newsitem.title: GERMANY: Adidas sales up sharply, but profit growth slows.
newsitem.headline: Adidas sales up sharply, but profit growth slows.

text.p: German sportswear company Adidas AG, reaping the benefits of an aggressive advertising campaign in North America, said Wednesday global sales rose at a double-digit pace in the second quarter, but profit growth slowed due to higher taxes.

Adidas said sales surged 37 percent in the second quarter, to 1.43 billion marks ($761 million). But net income rose only 20 percent from a year ago, to 69 million marks ($36.7 million), dampened by income tax payments that were more than double year-ago levels.
In the first quarter of 1997, profits totalled 169 million marks ($90 million).

Adidas said the tax payments, which totalled 34 million marks ($18 million), were due to a deferred tax charge of about five million marks ($2.7 million) in the second quarter and rising profits in high-tax countries, mainly in the Asia-Pacific region and Europe.
For the first half of the year, Adidas said its net income rose 29 percent to 238 million marks ($127 million), while sales were up 40 percent to 3.14 billion marks ($1.67 billion).

Adidas said apparel remained the major growth driver in the first six months of 1997. Apparel sales rose 55 percent in the period, while footwear rose 29 percent, helped by strong sales of running shoes.
But sales of basketball shoes, one of the largest segments of the U.S. sportswear market, remained weak, falling 50 percent in the first half of 1997.
"We are not performing in basketball where I would like to be," Adidas chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said.
Sales in North America, where Adidas has sought to take on global leaders Nike and Reebok on their home turf, grew 51 percent during the first half of the year to 727 million marks ($387 million).
Adidas said sales also got a boost from the weak mark against the dollar, but the company warned that strength in the dollar could start to hurt profit margins in 1998.

Adidas has signed a number of major sponsorship deals in the United States, including one with the New York Yankees baseball team, to boost its market share to 10 to 15 percent by the year 2000 from its 1996 level of about 5 percent.

Other notable high-profile sponsorship deals in the United States include professionl basketball star Kobe Bryant of the Los Angeles Lakers and college sports teams at Northwestern University and the University of Notre Dame.
